diagnosis: Post-Myocardial Infarction Pericarditis (Dressler Syndrome / Peri-infarct Pericarditis)

patient.key: Patient with recent MI, now on aspirin + clopidogrel + atenolol + atorvastatin. Presents with new chest pain. The ECG shows diffuse ST elevation, PR depression — classic pericarditis pattern. But this is a post-MI patient. The question: is this re-infarction or pericarditis?

correctlyAvoided: All NSAIDs (celecoxib, diclofenac, ibuprofen, indomethacin, naproxen, ketorolac, etc.) — contraindicated in post-MI pericarditis. Aspirin is the exception.
correctlyOrdered: EKG 12-lead (diffuse ST elevation + PR depression = pericarditis pattern, not STEMI)
Aspirin therapy + acetaminophen for pain control
Continued current post-MI medications (atenolol, clopidogrel, atorvastatin) — not discontinued

missedOrders.why: Post-MI patient with new chest pain = rule out re-infarction FIRST before calling it pericarditis. Troponin tells you if there's ongoing myocardial necrosis. Pericarditis itself can cause mild troponin elevation, but a significant rise or trend upward changes management entirely.
New chest pain in post-MI patient needs a CXR. Ruled out pneumothorax, pleural effusion, widened mediastinum. Pericarditis can cause a pericardial effusion visible on CXR.
Recent invasive procedure (cardiac cath for MI) = infection risk. Leukocytosis would raise concern for infectious pericarditis rather than post-MI autoimmune pericarditis.
Basic labs for any chest pain admission. Renal function matters for medication dosing.
Activity triggers recurrence of pericarditis symptoms. Rest until symptoms resolve prevents re-triggering the inflamed pericardium.

optional.why: Controversial in post-MI pericarditis — limited studies showing effectiveness. Not required and does not affect grade. Standard for idiopathic/viral pericarditis but evidence is thin in post-MI setting.

pathophysiology.postMiPericarditis: Autoimmune-mediated inflammation of the pericardium occurring days to weeks after myocardial infarction. The damaged myocardium exposes cardiac antigens → autoimmune response → immune complex deposition in the pericardium → inflammation. This is Dressler syndrome (weeks later) or peri-infarct pericarditis (days later). The mechanism is NOT infectious and NOT ischemic — it's the immune system attacking pericardial tissue that shares antigens with the infarcted myocardium.
pathophysiology.ekgPattern: Diffuse ST elevation (not territorial like STEMI) + PR depression. The PR depression is key: in STEMI, the PR segment is normal. In pericarditis, atrial inflammation causes PR depression. The ST elevation is diffuse (II, III, aVF, V2-V6) rather than confined to a single coronary territory.
pathophysiology.nsaidsContraindication: NSAIDs (except aspirin) inhibit COX-2, which impairs myocardial scar formation and ventricular remodeling after MI. They also increase cardiovascular thrombotic risk. In post-MI patients, NSAIDs are associated with increased mortality and re-infarction. Aspirin is the exception because it inhibits COX-1 (antiplatelet) at low doses, which is actually protective post-MI.
pathophysiology.aspirinVsNsaids: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 in platelets → blocks thromboxane A2 → antiplatelet effect. This is why aspirin is part of the post-MI regimen. NSAIDs reversibly inhibit COX-1 and COX-2 → block prostaglandin synthesis → analgesic/anti-inflammatory but also block prostacyclin (endothelial protection) → pro-thrombotic state post-MI. The distinction is pharmacologic, not semantic.

teachingPoints: Post-MI chest pain ALWAYS gets troponin first. Even if the ECG looks like pericarditis. Re-infarction kills. Pericarditis hurts but is self-limited. You prove it's not the one that kills before you treat the one that hurts.
NSAIDs are contraindicated post-MI. Aspirin is the exception. This is a high-yield USMLE concept: COX-2 inhibition impairs myocardial healing.
Colchicine is optional in post-MI pericarditis. In idiopathic pericarditis, it's standard of care (reduces recurrence). In post-MI, evidence is thin — the case says optional and not graded.
Pericarditis ECG: diffuse ST elevation + PR depression. STEMI ECG: territorial ST elevation, reciprocal changes, no PR depression. The PR segment tells you which one it is.
This case rewards restraint. Don't over-investigate (no cath lab for pericarditis). Don't over-treat (no NSAIDs, no colchicine required). Aspirin + acetaminophen + rest = correct management.
